Learning Objectives
Describe the basic physics of MRI.
Recognize the advantages and disadvantages of different magnetic types and field strengths.
Predict the appearance of different tissues on T1-weighted, T2-weighted, proton density, fat-
suppressed, and contrast-enhanced pulse sequences.
Compare MRI and CT.
List indications for magnetic resonance arthrography.
Review indications for metal-artifact reduction techniques.
List examples of common implanted devices and objects that are unsafe in the MRI scanner
area (termed MR unsafe), and list diagnostic tests and available resources to aid in making this
determination.
Review the common components of MRI contrast agents and indications and contraindications
for the use of MRI contrast.

General Principles
Scanner Physics
MRI is a tomographic imaging technique that uses a strong magnet and radiofrequency pulses
to create images.
Magnet strength is expressed in tesla (T) units.
Magnetic field strength is directly correlated with intrinsic signal-to-noise ratio and is the best
overall indicator of the image quality the MRI scanner can produce (Figure 1).
Low-field strength: 0.2 to 0.3T
Mid-field strength: 0.5 to 1.0T
High-field strength: ?1.5T
Figure 1 MRIs of the shoulder of a 53-year-old man with shoulder pain. Short tau inversion
recovery coronal (A) and sagittal (B) 0.2T MRIs show a low signal intensity (arrows) in the distal
supraspinatus tendon but no full-thickness tear. C, T2-weighted coronal 1.5T MRI shows a
small full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tear (arrow) that was confirmed via arthroscopy.
(Reproduced with permission from Magee T, Shapiro M, Williams D: Comparison of high-field-
strength versus low-field-strength MRI of the shoulder. AJR Am J Roentgenol 2003;81[5]:1211-
1215.)
Radiofrequency signals are applied to patient tissues in a pattern called a pulse sequence.

Scanner Physics
MRI is a tomographic imaging technique that uses a strong magnet and radiofrequency
pulses to create images. Tomography is defined as a method of producing a sequential
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:00 AM
AAOS | Magnetic Resonance Imaging
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004010
2/26

series of two-dimensional images of the internal structure of a solid object by passing an
energy wave through it and measuring the energy change. The MRI scanner produces
radiofrequency irradiation, which is absorbed by the body part of interest. The
radiofrequency signal emitted from the patient is detected by the scanner coils, which
function as antennae, converting the radiofrequency signal to an electrical current. This
data is processed by a computer to create images.11
Magnet strength is expressed in tesla (T) units. The field strength is directly correlated
with intrinsic signal-to-noise ratio. Magnets up to 3T routinely are used clinically, with
higher field strengths reserved for research. Up to 3T, field strength is the best overall
indicator of the image quality the scanner can produce (Figure 1). High-field strength (?
1.5T) is preferred.1,7 The higher field strength magnets can produce images faster but
are more prone to artifact. Imaging at 3T often, but not always, is better than imaging at
1.5T.
Image Contrast
Image contrast is affected by the pulse sequence parameters, most importantly the repetition
time and echo time.
The most common pulse sequences for musculoskeletal applications are T1-weighted, T2-
weighted, and proton density sequences (Table 1; Figure 2).


Image Contrast
Radiofrequency signals are applied to patient tissues in a pattern called a pulse
sequence. Image contrast is affected by the pulse-sequence parameters. Two important
parameters are the repetition time and the echo time. The most common pulse
sequences for musculoskeletal applications are T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and proton
density sequences11,12 (Table 1; Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:00 AM
AAOS | Magnetic Resonance Imaging
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004010
5/26

T1-weighted sequences use a short repetition time and short echo time. They are used
to demonstrate anatomy and to evaluate bone marrow (in cases of osteomyelitis and
bone tumors or other marrow replacing disorders).
T2-weighted sequences use a long repetition time and long echo time. They are used to
detect pathology, which often is associated with fluid because of hyperemia,
extracapsular leakage of joint fluid, soft-tissue edema, and hematoma formation.
Proton density sequences use a short repetition time and long echo time. These images
have the highest signal-to-noise ratio of any sequence, demonstrate anatomy well, and
are especially good for evaluating articular cartilage. They also are fluid sensitive, making
them helpful for the detection of pathology. Therefore, proton density MRI is the
workhorse of musculoskeletal imaging.11
Note that fat appears bright on all pulse sequences, is prevalent in the body, and
frequently obscures abnormal fluid signal or enhancement, which also appear bright on
T2-weighted and T1-weighted MRIs, respectively. Therefore, fat signal often is
suppressed, rendering pathologic signal more conspicuous. These sequences are called
short tau inversion recovery, T2-weighted fat-saturated, or proton density fat-saturated
MRIs.11 On T1-weighted MRI, this sequence is called a T1-weighted fat-saturated MRI and
usually is used if contrast is administered. Dixon is an imaging technique that involves
chemical shift to create uniform fat suppression and can be combined with various
tissue weightings, including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, proton density, and gradient echo
sequences.11 Gradient echo sequences can be rapidly acquired and detect hemosiderin
and calcifications, causing them to appear dark (low signal) and increase their size and
conspicuity, which is termed blooming.3 Metal causes artifact on these sequences and
renders them useless in the area of the metal.
Zero echo time or ultrashort echo time sequences are novel techniques for creating CT-
like contrast for bone4,5 (Figure 3).
MRI examinations consist of multiple pulse sequences in orthogonal planes designed to
evaluate the area of concern, called protocols. They are specific to the body part of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:00 AM
AAOS | Magnetic Resonance Imaging
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004010
6/26

interest and the suspected pathology indicated by the referring physician. The
sequences often used will change depending on the indication. For example, different
protocols will be used to image the ankle for a suspected ligament tear compared with
protocols used to image the ankle if concern for osteomyelitis exists. An accurate clinical
history is critical for the radiologist to optimize the examination protocol. MRI
postprocessing capabilities often are limited. If imaging of another area is desired later,
the patient must be reimaged, even if the areas are in proximity. For example, if a
patient’s shoulder were scanned, images of the elbow could not be constructed from the
data.
Characteristics of MRI Technique
MRI is associated with high soft-tissue contrast and high spatial resolution.
Dissimilar from CT, MRI involves no ionizing radiation.
Compared with CT, MRI is associated with relatively long examination times.
Enclosed machines cause claustrophobia in a minority of patients.
MRI is prone to artifact: metal, motion, and many others.
The contrast material for MRI is gadolinium-based.

Characteristics of MRI Technique
MRI produces images with excellent contrast and spatial resolution.11,14,15 Because of
its intrinsic high contrast, the use of intravenous contrast material is not necessary for
most examinations. The other main advantage of MRI is that it does not involve the use
of ionizing radiation; therefore, it is not associated with cancer risk to patients.13
Unfortunately, examination times are relatively long, and the patient must enter a
cylindrical bore, which induces claustrophobia in approximately 20% of patients. Most of
the time, the experience is manageable; however, extremely claustrophobic and young
pediatric patients will require sedation. MRI is prone to artifact, most commonly because
of patient motion and metal but also because of patient characteristics (eg, muscular
patients may be difficult to image at 3T). Artifact may substantially degrade image quality
unless countered via special techniques.8,27
MRI involves the use of contrast material that is gadolinium-based; gadolinium is a heavy
metal. It is regarded as extremely safe and can be injected intravenously or into joints

with those of CT in Table 2.

Types of MRI Scanners
Three types of MRI scanners exist. The most common and preferred scanner type is
conventional MRI (Figure 4, A). The patient is placed on a moveable table that slides in
and out of a cylindrical bore. Field strength ranges from 0.5 to 3T. Higher field strengths
are available but are primarily used for research. This scanner configuration is preferred
and tends to produce the best image quality. Newer scanner designs have a wider bore
(70 cm) than those in the past and can accommodate larger and more claustrophobic
patients. Open scanners offer even more space for the patient (Figure 4, B). Because of
scanner geometry, image quality suffers (Figure 5). Extremity scanners are much smaller
than the other two types of scanners, and only the extremity of interest is inserted
(Figure 4, C). Lower field strengths generally are needed, and these scanners are better
tolerated by those unable to lie flat, severely claustrophobic individuals, and younger
children. The main drawback of this design is that the spine and root joints, such as the
hip and shoulder, cannot be imaged.2 MRI scanner types are compared in Table 3.

Special Techniques
Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
Commonly used to augment MRI diagnosis of certain types of tears
Diluted gadolinium-based contrast is percutaneously injected into the joint. A tear is diagnosed
if contrast insinuates into the tear defect.
Common indications
Diagnosis of labral tears in the shoulder and hip joints
Diagnosis of triangular fibrocartilage complex and intrinsic ligament tears of the wrist
Diagnosis of medial collateral ligament tears of the elbow
Postoperative evaluation of a repaired meniscus

Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
Magnetic resonance arthrography is commonly used to augment MRI diagnosis of
certain types of tears. Diluted gadolinium-based contrast is percutaneously injected into
the joint. This is an off-label use.10 A tear is diagnosed if contrast insinuates into the tear
defect (Figure 6). The most common indication is the diagnosis of labral tears in the
shoulder and hip joints. Some controversy exists with regard to whether arthrography is
necessary to diagnose labral tears because routine shoulder and hip MRI is considered
adequate in most patients.17 For the shoulder, magnetic resonance arthrography is
considered the preferred imaging modality but is invasive.6,16,18 For the hip, magnetic
resonance arthrography is considered to be superior to routine MRI by some surgeons;
however, some data suggest that a 3T examination is equivalent.19,25 Magnetic
resonance arthrography also is used to diagnose triangular fibrocartilage complex and
intrinsic ligament tears of the wrist and medial collateral ligament tears of the elbow.

Magnetic Resonance Angiography
Produces images of the central and peripheral vessels
Techniques exist with and without the use of intravenous contrast.
Indications include evaluation for pseudoaneurysm, vascular malformation, vasculitis, and
tumor vascularity.

cartilage are among several techniques that attempt to provide microstructural information
about articular cartilage integrity before a defect is visible on conventional pulse
sequences20,21 (Figure 7; Resource 1).

Magnetic Resonance Neurography

Magnetic resonance neurography is the term used for directed imaging of peripheral
nerves. MRI enables direct visualization of the peripheral nervous system. The small size
of nerves often warrants using a 3T magnet and high-contrast three-dimensional
sequences, available from major vendors (Figure 8). This high-resolution technique
allows for diagnosis and characterization of intrinsic abnormalities, such as neuritis and
intraneural masses, and extrinsic compression or invasion by adjacent structures.22,23 In
addition, conventional sequences will demonstrate indirect signs of nerve pathology,
such as muscle denervation in a characteristic nerve distribution. Common applications
include imaging of the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses and imaging of individual
peripheral nerves (Resource 2).
Figure 8 Coronal, maximum intensity projection, T2-weighted, fat-suppressed magnetic
resonance neurogram of a normal brachial plexus (arrows). (Courtesy of Meghan Sahr,
MD, New York, NY.)

Screening MRI of the whole body can be achieved.
Indications include screening for cancer and multifocal inflammatory conditions, such as
myositis and chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis.
Especially favorable in children because of small body size and avoidance of ionizing radiation
from alternative imaging modalities (radiography, nuclear medicine, and positron emission
tomography CT)
Metal-Artifact Reduction
Metal objects create extensive artifact on MRIs.
Susceptibility artifact is mitigated and occasionally eliminated by metal-artifact reduction
techniques.
Basic methods should be used to reduce metal artifact.
Additional specific metal-artifact reduction sequences are available from vendors, occasionally
at an additional cost. These proprietary pulse sequences further reduce metal artifact and
have names such as slice-encoding for metal artifact correction and multi-acquisition variable-
resonance image combination.
Currently, MRI is commonly used for the diagnosis of bone and soft-tissue complications of
joint replacement (Figure 9).

the polyethylene post (arrows). B, Multi-acquisition variable-resonance image combination,
proton density MRI shows reduced artifact to the extent that the post is visible (dashed arrow).
C, Axial proton density MRI shows the prosthesis-bone interface and loosening (arrows) of the
patellar component. (Courtesy of Hollis Potter, New York, NY.)


Metal-Artifact Reduction
In the past, susceptibility artifact generated by orthopaedic hardware and arthroplasty
prostheses rendered MRI nondiagnostic. MRI manufacturers have developed techniques
that reduce and occasionally eliminate this artifact; however, image contrast is reduced.
Basic methods to reduce metal artifact are used together to perform a metal-artifact
reduction sequence, which is available on most clinical scanners. Some manufacturers
have developed proprietary pulse sequences that further reduce metal artifact.
Currently, MRI often is used for the diagnosis of bone and soft-tissue complications of
joint replacement8,26 (Figure 8).
Considerations in Pregnant Women
MRI does not involve the use of ionizing radiation; therefore, it is preferred over CT in pregnant
patients.
Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) cross the placenta and are excreted by the fetal
kidney into the amniotic fluid.
GBCA administration is not recommended in pregnant patients.

Considerations in Pregnant Woman
MRI does not involve the use ionizing radiation; therefore, it is preferred over CT in
pregnant patients. Risks of magnetic field and radiofrequency irradiation to the fetus are
considered theoretic and unknown and should be balanced against clinical need. The
preponderance of data shows no deleterious effects on a developing fetus at clinical
field strengths. GBCAs cross the placenta and are excreted by the fetal kidney into the
amniotic fluid. The long-term effects of fetal gadolinium exposure are unknown;
therefore, GBCA administration is not recommended in pregnant patients.10
Gadolinium-based Contrast Agents
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:00 AM
AAOS | Magnetic Resonance Imaging
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004010
19/26

GBCAs accumulate in highly vascular and metabolically active tissues if intravenously injected.
These areas appear bright on T1-weighted images, which is called enhancement.
Low rate of adverse reactions (0.07% to 2.4%)
Avoid if patients have a history of severe allergic-like reactions, such as anaphylaxis.
Some gadolinium contrast agents are contraindicated in patients with renal insufficiency.
Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a rare and atypical but serious fibrosing condition directly
related to intravenous GBCA administration in patients with severe acute or chronic renal
insufficiency (glomerular filtration rate <30 mg/dL). The condition is associated with some,
but not all, gadolinium contrast agents.
In patients with normal renal function, trace amounts of gadolinium are deposited within the
soft tissues, including the brain.
MRI with intravenous GBCA should only be ordered if diagnostically necessary.

Gadolinium-based Contrast Agents
GBCA accumulates in highly vascular and metabolically active tissues if intravenously
injected. These areas appear bright on T1-weighted images, which is called
enhancement. Dissimilar from CT, magnetic resonance contrast usually is not necessary
because of the intrinsically superior soft-tissue contrast on unenhanced examinations.
GBCA may be useful for the diagnosis and characterization of tumors, demyelinating
disease, and soft-tissue infection.
A low rate of adverse reactions has been reported after intravenous administration of
GBCA (0.07% to 2.4%). Prior mild allergic-like reactions are an indication for
corticosteroid prophylaxis prescribed by the ordering provider. In patients with a history
of severe allergic-like reaction, such as anaphylaxis, GBCA should be avoided.
Certain types of gadolinium contrast media are contraindicated in patients with renal
insufficiency. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a rare but serious fibrosing condition
primarily involving the skin and subcutaneous tissues. It may cause contractures leading
to immobility; may involve organs, such as the lungs, esophagus, heart, and skeletal
muscle; and occasionally is fatal. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is directly related to
intravenous administration of some types of GBCA in patients with severe acute kidney
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:00 AM
AAOS | Magnetic Resonance Imaging
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004010
20/26

injury or chronic renal failure (glomerular filtration rate <30 mg/dL). In patients with
normal renal function, trace amounts of gadolinium are deposited within the soft
tissues, including the brain. To date, no clinical evidence suggests that gadolinium
deposition is harmful to patients; however, numerous patient-created social media
groups claim adverse health effects related to GBCA. MRI with intravenous GBCA should
only be ordered if diagnostically necessary.10
Safety
Projectiles
All MRI scanners contain a strong magnet that is always on.
Ferromagnetic objects brought into the scanner room can turn into dangerous projectiles.
Patients and staff have suffered serious injury and death from these projectiles.
If a patient requires medical attention, even resuscitation, they should first be removed from
the scanner area.

Projectiles
All MRI scanners contain a strong magnet that is always on. Ferromagnetic objects
brought into the scanner room can turn into dangerous projectiles. If a medical
emergency occurs in the MRI scanner room, these objects may include surgical tools,
oxygen tanks, intravenous poles, and crash carts that are not labeled as magnetic
resonance safe. Patients and staff have suffered serious injury and death from these
projectiles. As an added safety measure, patients should be removed from the
scanner area before resuscitation is attempted.9,24
Foreign Bodies and Medical Implants
Unknown intraocular metallic foreign bodies in metal workers may migrate during scanning,
causing blindness.
Screening radiographs of the orbits can be obtained before MRI in these patients.

MRI is contraindicated in patients with some implanted medical devices, which may
malfunction in the magnetic field or cause tissue heating and a serious burn.
Most joint prostheses and orthopaedic hardware are magnetic resonance safe at clinical field
strengths, even in the immediate postoperative period.
Examples of magnetic resonance–unsafe devices include the following:
Cochlear implants
Nerve stimulators
Insulin pumps
Some pacemakers, stents, and filters
Older aneurysm clips (before 1995)
Some external fixator components
A history of an uneventful MRI is not sufficient evidence that the device is safe.

Foreign Bodies and Medical Implants
Unknown intraocular metallic foreign bodies in metal workers may migrate during
scanning, causing blindness. Screening plain radiographs of the orbits can be obtained
before MRI in these patients.
MRI is contraindicated in patients with some implanted medical devices, which may
malfunction in the magnetic field or cause tissue heating and a serious burn. Surgeons
should understand the magnetic resonance safety profile of hardware and implants
routinely used—information that is provided by the manufacturer. Examples of magnetic
resonance–unsafe devices include cochlear implants, nerve stimulators, insulin pumps,
some pacemakers, stents, filters, and older aneurysm clips. Arthroplasty prostheses,
orthopaedic hardware, certain newer pacemakers, and external fixators fall into an
intermediate safety category, termed magnetic resonance–conditional. This means they
may be scanned via MRI if the manufacturing and institution guidelines are carefully
followed.

Most joint prostheses and orthopaedic hardware are magnetic resonance safe at clinical
field strengths, even in the immediate postoperative period. Using MRI in patients with
an external fixator is a challenge because external fixators are composed of numerous
parts, some of which may be safe and some of which may not be safe. Specific guidelines
vary by manufacturer and may preclude placing the fixator within the bore of the
magnet, prohibit the use of a specialized extremity coil, or forbid the inclusion of certain
components. If the manufacturer is unknown, some institutions will test attraction to a
common magnet and proceed with imaging if no attraction occurs; however, practice
and policy vary. In other cases, external fixators may simply generate too much artifact
to generate a diagnostic study. Manufacturer literature has cited a zone of
approximately 6 cm around the hardware that will be obscured, which may be larger or
smaller in clinical practice, depending on the metal artifact reduction technology on the
scanner.
MRI technologists and radiologists routinely screen patients for implanted devices;
however, the referring physician can help by instructing the patient to obtain records
documenting the exact device implanted in advance of imaging. A history of an
uneventful MRI is not sufficient evidence that the device is safe. Conversely, avoidance of
MRI based only on the presence of an implanted device without investigation may
deprive the patient of the best imaging modality available. Resource 3 includes an
extensive list of the magnetic resonance safety profile of medical devices. If in doubt, ask
the radiology department.9,24
